claim: Our CIFAR-10 model achieves a test error rate of 3.65, which is 0.09 percent better and 1.05x faster than the previous state-of-the-art model that used a similar architectural scheme.
evidence: The DenseNet model that achieves 3.46% error rate (Huang et al., 2016b) uses 1x1 convolutions to reduce its total number of parameters, which we did not do, so it is not an exact comparison.

claim: Our method achieves an improvement of 1.3 BLEU from the previous best models on both WMT’14 and WMT’15 English→German.
evidence: Our model obtains an improvement of 1.3 BLEU from the previous best models on both WMT’14 and WMT’15 English→German.

claim: Our evaluation of these neural network topologies indicates asynchronous gradient descent has a speedup of up to 1.7x compared to synchronous.
evidence: Specifically, the best asynchronous approach is up to 1.7x faster than the synchronous approach while achieving up to 82% parallel efficiency.

claim: Our agent significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art on Atari, averaging 880% expert human performance, and a challenging suite of first-person, three-dimensional Labyrinth tasks leading to a mean speedup in learning of 10× and averaging 87% expert human performance on Labyrinth.
evidence: The UNREAL agent, which combines all three auxiliary tasks, achieves more than twice the final human-normalised mean performance of A3C, increasing from 54% to 87% (45% to 92% for median performance).

claim: Results showed a squared error is reduced to 1/25 that of a conventional method .
evidence: Competitive learning was applied to supervised learning and the squared error was reduced to 1/25 that of a conventional method.

claim: While the inference procedure is not operating on top of observed instances for IRNs, our proposed model outperforms all previous approaches on the popular FB15k benchmark by more than 5.7%.
evidence: • We evaluate IRNs and demonstrate that our proposed model achieves the state-of-the-art results on the popular FB15k benchmark, surpassing prior approaches by more than 5.7%.

claim: On the Stanford question answering dataset, a single DCN model improves the previous state of the art from 71.0% F1 to 75.9%, while a DCN ensemble obtains 80.4% F1.
evidence: On the SQuAD dataset, the DCN achieves the state of the art results at 75.9% F1 with a single model and 80.4% F1 with an ensemble.

claim: We validate our model on a simplified memory copy task and see that our model can learn dependencies as long as 5,000 timesteps.
evidence: We evaluate our approach on a simplified 1-bit version of the memory copying task, and find that our architecture can scale to 5,000 timesteps on this task, outperforming past approaches.
